'''Walter Charles Marshall, Baron Marshall of Goring''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|CBE|FRS}}<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Fishlock | first1 = D. | last2 = Roberts | first2 = L. E. J. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1998.0020  | doi-access = free| title = Walter Charles Marshall, C. B. E., Lord Marshall of Goring. 5 March 1932-20 February 1996 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 44 | pages = 299–312 | year = 1998 }}</ref> (5 March 1932 – 20 February 1996)<ref name=Indy>{{cite news |last=Baker |first=John |date= 26 September 1996|title=Obituary: Lord Marshall of Goring |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/obituary-lord-marshall-goring-5626891.html |work=The Independent |location= |access-date= }}</ref> was a noted theoretical physicist and leader in the UK's energy sector.

==Early life==
{{more citations needed section|date=September 2021}}
The son of Frank Marshall and Amy Pearson, he attended the [[grammar school]] St Illtyd's Boys College 
(now [[St Illtyd's Catholic High School]]).

He studied mathematical physics at [[Birmingham University]] and gained a PhD there<ref name=Indy/> under [[Rudolf Peierls]].

==Career==
He joined the Theoretical Physics Division at [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment|AERE Harwell]] in 1954, succeeding [[Brian Flowers]] as Head of that Division in 1960 and becoming Director of AERE in 1968; he eventually was appointed Chairman of the [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]] in 1981.<ref name=Indy/>

===CEGB===
As a champion of [[nuclear power]], he was appointed, in 1983, to be chairman of the [[Central Electricity Generating Board]]. He was also highly sceptical of [[fusion power]], famously noting that "fusion is an idea with infinite possibility and zero chance of success."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parkins |first1=William E. |last2=Krumhansl |first2=James A. |last3=Starr |first3=Chauncey |date=1997 |title=Insurmountable Engineering Problems Seen as Ruling out 'Fusion Power to the People' in 21st Century |url=http://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.881707 |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=15–102 |doi=10.1063/1.881707 |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Parkins |first=W. E. |date=1978-03-31 |title=Engineering Limitations of Fusion Power Plants: Problems related to radiation damage and plant costs may prevent the practical application of fusion. |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.199.4336.1403 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=199 |issue=4336 |pages=1403–1408 |doi=10.1126/science.199.4336.1403 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 1989, with the government's plan to reorganise and privatise electricity generation, the position of Chairman of the CEGB disappeared. He was made Chairman of National Power which included a large number of the coal- and oil-fired power stations and all of the nuclear power stations. National Power was a division of the CEGB until it was privatised in 1990. This was done as he had a close association with nuclear power, from the early years. But before the privatisation process was complete, the city was not happy with the nuclear component in National Power, and it was removed from the process and placed into another state-owned company (only to be part privatised some 5 years later). It was as a result of this political decision that he resigned his post as Chairman of National Power. Marshall then entered into several jobs in the private sector connected with the nuclear industry and died in 1996.

As a scientist, Marshall was recognised as one of the leading theoreticians in the atomic properties of matter and characterised by his penetrating analytical powers. He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1971.<ref name="frs"/> In 1977 he was elected a foreign member of the [[Royal Swedish Academy of Engineering Sciences]].

In 1981 he chaired a Task Force, set up with representatives from major interested parties to evaluate the basis for the Sizewell B Design of nuclear power station.<ref>{{cite book |title=Nuclear Lessons Learned |date=October 2010 |publisher=The Royal Academy of Engineering |isbn=978-1-903496-60-2 |page=14 |url=https://www.raeng.org.uk/publications/reports/nuclear-lessons-learned |access-date=16 August 2019}}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1955 he married Ann Sheppard in [[Cardiff]] and had a son and daughter.<ref name=Indy/>

Appointed a [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) in 1973,<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=45860 |date=1 January 1973 |page=8 |supp=y}}</ref> he was [[Knight Bachelor|Knighted]] in the [[1982 Birthday Honours]].<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=49008|page=2|date=11 June 1982|supp=y}}</ref><ref>{{London Gazette |issue=49120 |date=24 September 1982 |page=12413}}</ref>

For his success in keeping the country's “lights on” during the protracted miners’ strike of 1984–5, [[Margaret Thatcher]] rewarded him with a [[life peerage]] and he became '''Baron Marshall of Goring''', of [[South Stoke, Oxfordshire|South Stoke]] in the County of [[Oxfordshire]] on 22 July 1985.<ref>{{London Gazette |issue=50208 |date=25 July 1985 |page=10221}}</ref>
